analysis.one_liner: Bans big companies from charging unconscionably excessive prices during emergencies.
analysis.headline: The price gouging ban never received a hearing or vote in either committee it was referred to, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: During an 'exceptional market shock' — a hurricane, war, energy shortage, or public-health emergency — the bill would make it unlawful for companies to charge unconscionably excessive prices, no matter where they sit in the supply chain. Companies with over $1 billion in US revenue would face a presumption of violation if their prices exceed their pre-shock averages, with penalties up to 5% of their parent company's annual US revenue. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could sue, publicly traded companies would have to disclose their profit margins and pricing strategies in filings after a shock quarter, and the FTC would get $1 billion in additional funding. Companies with under $100 million in revenue are exempt if they can show price increases only reflect their own added costs.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers during emergencies: people filling gas tanks before a hurricane, buying groceries or medicine during a shortage, or paying utility bills after a disruption would gain a federal backstop against opportunistic price spikes. Small businesses (under $100 million in revenue) benefit from an explicit exemption with a cost-based defense, and state attorneys general gain a new federal tool to sue on behalf of their residents.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers hit by emergency price spikes

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any seller, at any level of the supply chain, to charge an unconscionably excessive price during an exceptional market shock such as a natural disaster, war, energy shortage, or public-health emergency [S3].

Creates a presumption of violation for large companies — those with at least $1 billion in US revenue or other market leverage — whose prices exceed their own or the market's average price from the 120 days before the shock; they can only rebut it with clear and convincing evidence that costs outside their control forced the increase [S3].
Lets the FTC and state attorneys general sue for injunctions, civil penalties, and restitution for consumers, and gives the FTC $1 billion in new funding to do the enforcement work [S3].

Requires publicly traded companies to disclose, in the filing after a shock quarter, how much of their revenue growth came from higher prices versus higher volume, their gross margins by product line, and a detailed explanation of their pricing strategy [S3].
Exempts companies whose ultimate parent earned under $100 million in US revenue, provided they show price increases directly reflect added costs they could not control [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations. Any company facing a violation could owe civil penalties up to 5% of its ultimate parent's annual US revenue, and publicly traded companies would bear new compliance costs to disclose margins, price-volume breakdowns, and pricing rationales to the SEC. Businesses between $100 million and $1 billion in revenue would face the ban without the large-company presumption but still carry the burden of proving their increases were cost-driven.

drawbacks.text: The ban could deter legitimate price increases during genuine supply crises: if a company raising prices to ration scarce goods (like fuel before a hurricane) risks a lawsuit and penalties up to 5% of parent revenue, some firms may hold prices low and let shelves empty instead — a real shortage-management concern an honest supporter must weigh [S3].

The bill's standards — 'unconscionably excessive,' 'excessive,' and what counts as a market — were left to FTC regulations due within 180 days, and the SEC was given only 60 days to write detailed margin-disclosure rules; deadlines that tight invite litigation over vague rules and rushed implementation [S3].

Companies between $100 million and $1 billion in revenue get no small-business exemption but also lack the clear $1 billion leverage threshold, leaving a middle band of firms to litigate what counts as an acceptable price increase after any shock [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the upside is concrete: a federal floor against price gouging during emergencies, private-profit disclosures that would show whether inflation-era price hikes reflected costs or margin expansion, and new state AG enforcement tools. The costs fall almost entirely on large corporations, though some of the design is rough — tight rulemaking deadlines, vague standards delegated to regulators, and a shortage-rationing risk during true supply collapses. A narrower version with longer implementation timelines would carry less risk of chilling legitimate pricing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees, but neither ever held a hearing or markup, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the bill on May 12, 2022, with seven original cosponsors, during a period of elevated inflation and energy prices [S3].

It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Financial Services Committee on the day of introduction; the action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote [S5].
It picked up 22 cosponsors, all Democrats, and never advanced in committee before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations avoided a federal price-gouging ban with penalties reaching 5% of parent-company revenue, and publicly traded companies avoided new profit-margin and pricing disclosures. The FTC did not receive the $1 billion in new enforcement funding.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large corporations that avoided the ban

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor — 23 members in total — was a House Democrat; no Republican signed on, and no Republican action is recorded either way.

industries.note: They would face a presumption of illegal price gouging during market shocks and civil penalties up to 5% of their parent's annual US revenue per violation. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against consumers' interest in price protection during emergencies.

The bill would force them to disclose margins, price-versus-volume revenue breakdowns, and pricing rationales after any shock quarter — transparency that investors and the public would use to judge whether price hikes reflected costs or profit-taking.
They are exempt from the ban if they can show price increases directly reflect uncontrollable added costs, so they could pass through genuine cost increases while large competitors faced penalties.
They would gain a new federal cause of action to sue price gougers for penalties and restitution on behalf of their residents, layered on top of existing state laws the bill explicitly preserves.
The FTC would get $1 billion in new funding, rulemaking authority to define the standards, and independent litigation power to seek injunctions, penalties, and consumer restitution.
